verses.text: Their road took them through Amphipolis and Apollonia— the great Roman highway — and brought them at last to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue.

Paul went in, as he always did, and for three Sabbaths running he reasoned with them out of the Scriptures.Not preaching down at them — arguing, opening the texts, taking their objections and answering them.

footnotes.content: Luke chooses this phrase deliberately. In his Gospel he used almost exactly these words for Jesus, who went to the synagogue on the Sabbath "as was his custom" (Luke 4:16). Paul is not leaving his Jewish life behind — he is continuing it. The way the announcement begins is inside the synagogue, not outside it.

verses.text: Passage by passage he laid it out: the Messiah had to go this way — through suffering, through death — and rise again. And every time, the same landing: "This Jesus I am telling you about — he is the Messiah."
Some of them were persuaded. They joined Paul and Silas, and so did a great many Greeks who worshiped the God of Israel— without being Jews themselves — and a good many of the city's leading women.

footnotes.keyword: Greeks who worshiped the God of Israel
footnotes.content: These were the "God-fearers" — a recognized category in the cities of the eastern Mediterranean: non-Jews who worshiped the one God of Israel and kept the ethical commandments of the Torah without formally converting. Inscriptions from Aphrodisias and Sardis name them explicitly. Many were women of social standing; with the framework of Israel's Scriptures already familiar to them, they were the readiest hearers the message could find.

verses.text: But the others — jealousy took them. They watched their own standing drain away toward a stranger: the trust, the circle of followers, everything that had been theirs. So they rounded up a few idlers from the marketplace, drew a crowd together, and threw the city into uproar. They stormed Jason's house, expecting to find Paul and Silas there and haul them out before the assembly.

footnotes.content: The Greek says "the Jews" stirred up the trouble. It means specific members of the Thessalonian synagogue — not the Jewish people. Paul is himself a Jew; so is Silas; the dispute runs inside Judaism, among Jews, over a messianic claim. For centuries Christian interpretation turned sentences like this into an accusation against "the Jews" as such — a reading that is false to the text, and that fed persecution and worse. This passage is the record of one local conflict, nothing more.

verses.text: They weren't there. So the mob seized Jason and a few of the believers instead, and dragged them before the politarchs, the city leaders, shouting: "The men who turned the empire upside down — they're here now too,

footnotes.content: "Politarch" was not common Greek — for a long time scholars treated the title as Luke's mistake, since it turned up nowhere else in ancient literature. Then archaeology produced more than thirty inscriptions across Macedonia naming exactly this office, nineteen of them from Thessalonica alone. It was the locally precise word for the city's elected board of magistrates, with the power to demand a bond from citizens and to pass cases up the Roman chain of command. Where other ancient writers grew vague, Luke knew the city.

verses.text: and Jason has taken them in. Every one of them defies Caesar's decrees. They say there is another king — Jesus."

footnotes.content: Under Roman law, proclaiming a rival ruler was treason — the gravest charge that could be brought. It is the exact accusation laid against Jesus before Pilate: that he claimed to be a king (Luke 23:2). What is striking is that the believers do not deny it. The narrator lets the charge stand, as though it were accidentally true: to call Jesus "king" is to re-order your loyalties — and every power built on loyalty can feel it.

verses.text: It was the most dangerous thing anyone could say in that city. The crowd shook, and the magistrates shook with them.
They made Jason and the others post bond— a pledge against further trouble — and only then let them go.

sections.heading: Beroea: A People Who Examined Day by Day

verses.text: That same night the believers sent Paul and Silas on to Beroea, off the main road. And there too, the first thing they did was go to the synagogue.

These were people of a different kind — more open-minded than the ones in Thessalonica. They took the message in eagerly, and did not stop there. Day after day they went back to the Scriptures and examined them, to see whether what they were hearing held up.

footnotes.content: The Greek word for this examining comes from the language of the courts: it means cross-examination, the testing of a claim against the evidence. The people of Beroea were not pious nodders — day after day they took up the Scriptures and held Paul's claims against them. And they did it together, in the synagogue, not each one alone. Where this verse was later made the banner of a "let everyone judge for themselves" individualism, what was lost was exactly what makes it remarkable: a shared, patient, argumentative reading, in which eagerness and rigor are not opposites.

What Beroea models is a way of reading that refuses the choice between enthusiasm and scrutiny. If you have ever assumed that taking a text seriously means switching off your judgment — or that asking hard questions means you have already left — this verse says otherwise: the people praised here are the ones who checked. You can start there, with nothing required of you but honesty: read a passage and ask, plainly, whether it holds. For those further along, the practice deepens when it becomes daily and shared — a fixed time, the same texts, and other people free to disagree with you, because a reading tested only against yourself is barely tested at all. And it reaches past the page. The Berean habit — claims held against the evidence, in company, over time — is also how a workplace stays honest, how a friendship survives a hard conversation, how a community keeps the loudest voice in the room from becoming the truest. This week, find one other person and read something together that you would otherwise have read alone.

verses.text: Many of them came to believe — Greek women of standing, and men, a good number of them.
It could have been a good place to stay. But when the Thessalonian opponents heard that Paul was announcing God's word in Beroea as well, they came after him there and stirred up the crowds.
At once the believers sent Paul on toward the sea, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind.
The men who went with Paul saw him the whole way to Athens. Then they started back, carrying an instruction: Silas and Timothy were to follow as soon as they could.

Paul waited for them in Athens. Silas and Timothy had not arrived yet, and so he had time to walk the city, a city that stood, like no other, for learning and philosophy. And what he saw gave him no peace. The city was full of idols— an altar at every corner, a god in every doorway, sacred stones wedged between the houses. The longer he looked, the less he could hold still.

So he reasoned with them. In the synagogue with Jews and with the Greeks who worshiped the God of Israel — and every day in the marketplace, with whoever happened to be there. Never a lecture. Always an argument.

Before long the philosophers took him on — followers of Epicurus, and Stoics. Some sneered: "What is this seed-picker trying to tell us?"— a bird hopping the market for crumbs, a scavenger of other people's scraps. Others said, "He seems to be announcing foreign gods." They said it because he was speaking about Jesus, and about resurrection.

footnotes.content: Two living schools of thought, not museum pieces. The Epicureans sought an unshakable calm: the world is made of atoms, the gods take no interest in us, and after death there is nothing — so live moderately, without fear. The Stoics sought virtue by aligning the self with the reason that runs through the whole cosmos. A Stoic could make something of talk about a God who is near. Neither school could do anything with the resurrection of the dead: for the one, the body is atom-dust; for the other, a prison the soul is glad to be free of.

verses.text: So they took him up to the Areopagus— the council that had always decided which new gods, which foreign cults, would be given a home in Athens. "May we know," they asked, "what this new teaching of yours is?

footnotes.content: The Areopagus was two things at once: a rocky hill below the Acropolis, and the council that met there. Once a court for cases of bloodshed, by Paul's day it watched over public order — including the question of which new gods and foreign cults the city would admit. Paul is not on a stage for free speech; he is in something closer to a hearing. There is an irony ancient listeners caught at once: the founding charter of this very court ruled a resurrection of the dead explicitly out — blood once spilled stays spilled. That is precisely where Paul will end.

verses.text: What you are telling us sounds strange to us, and we would like to understand what it means."
For the Athenians, and the foreigners who had settled among them, loved nothing so much as telling, or hearing, the latest thing.

So Paul stood up in their midst, there in the middle of the council, and began. "Men of Athens. Everywhere I look in this city, I can see how seriously you take the gods, and how thoroughly the divine has been worked into the texture of your common life.

footnotes.keyword: how seriously you take the gods
footnotes.content: The Greek word here can be read two ways — "superstitious," or "genuinely religious, serious about the divine." Older translations often chose the insult. But Paul is opening a speech by the rules of ancient oratory, and such an opening is built to win the audience's goodwill — it does not begin with a slap. The sense is the generous one: you take the divine with great seriousness. We translate what Paul is doing: he honors his hearers' search before he carries it further.

verses.text: For as I walked through your city and looked closely at the things you worship, I came at last upon an altar with these words cut into its stone: to an unknown god. What you worship, then, without knowing it — that is what I have come to tell you.

footnotes.content: Athenian devotion covered every angle. The travel-writer Pausanias describes altars "to unknown gods"; similar ones are attested elsewhere. The logic was protective: lest a god you have failed to honor turn against you, you build it an altar in advance. Paul takes up that gesture — and sharpens it, turning the many unknown gods into a single one. He does not mock the altar. He takes seriously the search inside it, and claims: what you sense without being able to name it, that I can name.

verses.text: The God who made the world and everything in it — the Lord of heaven and earth — does not live in temples built by human hands,
nor is he served by human hands, as though he stood in need of anything; he is himself the one who gives every living thing its life, its breath, all that it has.
From one he made every people of the earth, and settled them across the whole face of it; he set the times appointed for them, and the boundaries of the lands where they live —

footnotes.content: The Greek manuscripts diverge here. The oldest read "from one"; many others read "from one blood." Both say the same decisive thing: every people descends from a single source, and no nation stands above another. The familiar English smoothing "from one man" is in no Greek manuscript at all. The verse has a bitter history: in nineteenth-century America, opponents of slavery appealed to it — "all of one blood" — and so did its defenders, twisting it the other way. The text itself knows no ranking of peoples.

verses.text: and all of it so that they would seek him, would reach out for him, the way a person feels for something in the dark, and perhaps in the end find him. Though the truth is, he is not far from any one of us.

footnotes.keyword: not far from any one of us
footnotes.content: This is the line of the chapter for the reader who is not, by their own reckoning, "arrived." Paul is not saying that the seekers among his audience are at the doorstep, almost-but-not-yet; he is saying that what they have been reaching for — by touch, in the half-light, without certainty — has never been at any real distance. The mode of search the verse honors is tactile, not analytical: not what one has worked out, but what one feels for in the dark. If you do not know what you believe, the verse speaks about you, not against you. A concrete way to take it up: one pause a day, thirty seconds, in which you do not try to settle the question — only let it stand, and let yourself be near it. And one person, this week, with whom you can say out loud the thing you would normally keep to yourself.

verses.text: For in him we live, and in him we move, and in him we have our being — as some of your own poets have said: We too are his children.

footnotes.content: The line is a quotation — from a poem by the Greek writer Aratus, who, like Paul, came from Cilicia. The earlier phrase, "in him we live and move," also had a ring that Stoic listeners would have recognized. What is remarkable is what Paul does with it: a Jewish messenger quotes pagan poetry, not to refute it but to agree with it. Greek wisdom, at its best, has touched something true; Paul takes it up and carries it forward. It is a generosity that later Christian argument too often lost.

verses.text: And if we are indeed his children, then we cannot suppose that what is divine in any way resembles gold or silver or stone — an image shaped by human craft and human imagination.
The times of not-knowing God let pass. But now he calls on everyone, everywhere, to turn— to repent.

footnotes.content: "Not-knowing" can sound dismissive — as if everything before faith were mere darkness. That is not the sense. Paul is speaking to an educated audience in the intellectual capital of the ancient world; the "not-knowing" he names is the religious confusion of that confident elite — the city of countless altars that still had to dedicate one to a god it could not name. It is not a blanket verdict on every non-Christian culture. Where the sentence was later used to write off other religions as plain darkness, that was a misuse of the text.

verses.text: For he has set a day on which he will judge the world, and judge it justly, through a man he has appointed; and the proof he has given, to all, is this: he raised that man from the dead."

footnotes.keyword: he raised that man from the dead
footnotes.content: This is where the speech breaks — then and now. A resurrection of the dead: for a modern, skeptical reader, this is the place to get off. The Christian tradition does not read this line as a naive boast, but as the hinge everything turns on. Paul does not argue the resurrection into being from first principles; he reports an event — something he says happened, attested by people who staked their lives on it. If it is true, it is not a pious ornament but the reason this movement exists at all: death, which had the last word for the old Athenians, does not have it here. That is a serious reading, not a credulous one. If the step to a historical event is too far for you, the text still says something: that a justice which counts is not handed down by the powerful, but by one whom the powerful killed — and that violence does not get the last word. And if even that is more than you can take, read on anyway — the Athenians themselves split at exactly this point: some laughed, some put it off. You are in good company if you hesitate. The question the text leaves open is not whether you must believe it all at once, but how far you are willing to go.

verses.text: At the words "raised from the dead," the meeting broke apart. Some of them laughed. Others said, "We will hear you on this another time."
And Paul left the council.
But some joined him and believed — Dionysius, a member of the council itself; a woman named Damaris; and others besides.

footnotes.content: Damaris is the only woman named among the converts at Athens — and one of the very few women anywhere in the New Testament to appear in a setting this learned and this public. For a long time it was assumed that a woman in such a place could only have been a courtesan. Recent scholarship — Ivoni Richter Reimer among others — has set that reading aside: more likely she was herself educated in philosophy, since the Epicurean and Pythagorean schools admitted women. One old family of manuscripts cut her name out entirely; the same tendency quietly weakens the standing of women elsewhere in Acts. Luke names her, equal to Dionysius. So do we.
